newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina blasts US on trade, nixes WTO complaint.
newsitem.headline: Argentina blasts US on trade, nixes WTO complaint.

text.p: Argentina Friday accused the United States of being "insatiable" in its demands for more patent protection, but said it would ignore calls to take the case to the World Trade Organization (WTO).
"Americans are insatiable," Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella told reporters, defending new patent legislation which has been denounced as inadequate by Washington. "They are always complaining."

The White House Tuesday announced it would withdraw trade benefits to Argentina over what President Clinton called inadequate intellectual property protection under the new laws, in particular for pharmaceuticals.

But Di Tella said President Carlos Menem's government -- which tried but failed to have Congress address the U.S. demands in the new law -- would ignore calls from legislators and government officials to file a complaint with the WTO.
"It would not be the right moment or opportunity, because moves under the Generalized System of Preferences (GSP) are not ruled by the WTO," Di Tella said. "It is a unilateral U.S. decision."

The White House says the 50 percent cut in the number of Argentine products that can be imported duty-free under GSP will affect $260 million worth of goods. Argentine businessmen said it will cost them a total $20 million a year in lost exports.

Ruling Peronist Party legislators have joined forces with opposition colleagues to demand an appeal to the WTO and retaliations. They call it a question of sovereignty and find the government's more cautious approach unsatisfactory.
"We believe we should go further," Wednesday said Humberto Roggero, Peronist chairman of the Industry Committee, which wants to exclude U.S. firms from privatizations while the sanctions last.
Di Tella insisted the new patent legislation meets international standards and said he has sent a letter to U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky.
Economy Ministry Coordination Secretary Julio Caceres has pledged to put the issue to U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley when he visits Argentina next month.

And Radical Party deputy Juan Pablo Baylac, vice-president of the lower house's Industry Committee which is united against the U.S. move, promised a cool welcome for the U.S. leader when he visits Argentina in October.
"Clinton will not find it very pleasant when he visits our country," he said.
